stories.title: 'I've caught one fish all season' - how a polluted river could end 300 years of coracle fishing
stories.summary: It is a centuries-old tradition in Wales, but coracle fishers on a major river have said pollution has meant there are "no fish" left. Testing by campaign group Save the River Tywi showed evidence of industrial, agricultural and human waste pollution, with fishers saying they often see dead fish bobbing up and down in the water. One fifth-generation coracle fisherman described the situation in Carmarthenshire as "dire" after only catching one fish in the three-month season between May and July. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it took all reports of pollution seriously and had "a number of ongoing enforcement and compliance investigations within the Tywi catchment". The tradition of coracle fishing has been part of life on the Tywi for centuries. Typically done at night, fishermen use small rounded boats with nets cast among them to catch salmon and sewin [sea trout]. It was once an important livelihood in west Wales, but today it is mostly a heritage tradition, rather than a full-time source of income. US President Jimmy Carter even loved fishing in these rivers, but according to fishermen, recent pollution has made it impossible. Chairman of Carmarthen Coracle and Netsman Association, Andrew Davies, said he thought the four coracle men on the Tywi had caught 12 fish among them in the whole of the 2026 season when, a few years ago, "you'd catch that many in a night". Keith Elias's family have been fishing on the river for 300 years - he said he had only caught one fish this season. "It's been in my family for so long, I love carrying the tradition on, but it's getting to the point where you get to the end of the season and you're not hitting fish. "You just don't want to go."

stories.title: Panama Canal to reduce shipping as El Niño fuels drought in lakes that feed waterway
stories.summary: The operator said it does not rule out further restrictions on shipping depending on how much it rains in the coming weeks. The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month because of drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, the operator of the strategic waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific said. From 3 September, the number of vessels allowed through each day will fall from 36 to 34 due to lower water levels in two artificial lakes that feed the canal, the Panama Canal Authority said. It will drop to 32 from 15 September onward, the agency said. Central America is in the throes of a severe drought driven by El Niño, a weather pattern that warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall. In the area of the canal rainfall from May to August is down by 34% from its historical average, the authority said, adding that El Niño could cut it even more. The Panama Canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and around 40% of US container traffic. The canal operator said that "lower than forecast rainfall in the canal's watershed" called for measures to bolster the "long-term sustainability" of the waterway. It has already implemented other water conservation measures, such as lowering the maximum draft, the vessel's depth in the water, for the largest ships. In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway's operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22. It said that with the upcoming reduction, waiting times for ships trying to get through without making a reservation beforehand will increase. Nine of 10 ships using the canal do so with a reservation and the remaining slots are auctioned off.
